children: Iron ore prices rose on Thursday, helped by hopes of improved demand as analysts expect steelmakers in top consumer China  to restock feedstocks from December.
The most-traded iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange
climbed 1.75% to 667.5 yuan ($100.00) a metric ton, as of 0209 GMT, after hitting its highest since November 16 at 669 yuan earlier in the session.
The benchmark January iron ore (SZZFF7) on the Singapore Exchange was 0.96% higher at $89.15 a ton, as of 0159 GMT.
The focus of trading has shifted to expectations of a flurry of feedstock restocking among steelmakers in December, sparking a price rebound, analysts at broker First Futures said in a note.

Raw material inventory at steel mills stayed low, so mills will start to replenish feedstocks from December, lending support to prices until the wave of replenishment is over, analysts at broker Yongan Futures said in a note.
"But there is still strong resistance at a level above 670 yuan," First Futures analysts added.
Chinese steelmakers typically stockpile feedstocks in winter in preparation for production needs over the week-long Lunar New Year holiday which falls in February next year.
Moreover, some mills have completed equipment maintenance, increasing their need for feedstocks.
Many mills have kept their in-plant raw material feedstock low amid thin profitability and tepid steel demand.
Other steelmaking ingredients extended gains with coking coal
and coke (DCJcv1) up 3.7% and 2.71%, respectively, supported by persistent worry about supply.
Steel benchmarks on the Shanghai Futures Exchange gained ground. Rebar
